# vkernels — low-level CUDA kernels and communication primitives

`vkernels` is the kernel layer for [opentela](https://github.com/opentela-ai): hand-tuned
CUDA kernels and the communication primitives (collectives, overlap, topology) that sit
beside them. Everything ships with a **CPU reference implementation** so it can be unit-tested
and measured for coverage on machines **without a GPU**, and a CUDA implementation that is
compiled automatically when a CUDA toolkit is present.

> **Documentation in depth:** the [project wiki](https://github.com/opentela-ai/vkernels/wiki)
> distills the engineering knowledge — the roofline method, the kernel optimization ladder,
> occupancy/latency findings, cross-architecture lessons (MI300A vs GB10 vs MI250X), numerics
> and oracle contracts, LDS layout, CUDA-graph capture rules, debugging case files, and the
> per-kernel catalog with gaps to speed of light.

The directory is empty, so this is a greenfield design question. Given what's in this repo — bit-exact oracle contracts, MXFP4 MoE, FP8 DSA indexer, sparse top-k attention, lossy-able comm paths — here's a catalog of relaxation techniques I'd suggest writing down, organized by *what gets relaxed*. Each has a bound form you can actually prove rather than just empirically observe.

## 1. Precision / roundoff relaxation

- **Reduced-precision inputs, fp32 accumulate** (bf16/fp16/fp8 MXFP4 GEMMs): every rounding contributes relative error ≤ u (unit roundoff: bf16 2⁻⁸, e4m3 ~2⁻⁴, e2m1 ~2⁻²). A K-term dot product is bounded by the Wilkinson bound **γ_K = Ku/(1−Ku)** · Σ|aᵢbᵢ| — *independent of summation order*, so the same bound covers split-K, tree reduction, atomics.
- **Reduction-order freedom** — your oracle contracts are currently "bit-identical to CPU reference". The γ_n bound is the principled replacement: any reordering of a sum satisfies |fl(Σx) − Σx| ≤ γ_{n−1}Σ|xᵢ|. Turns "must match exactly" into a *tolerance class with a derivation*, which is exactly the contract a GPU kernel can honor (FMA contraction, different tile splits, atomics).
- **Rounding mode / FTZ**: RTZ instead of RTNE at most doubles the bound; flush-to-zero has a small *absolute* bound (min subnormal), not relative — fine for activations, dangerous for losses.
- **Stochastic rounding**: unbiased (E[fl(Σx)] = Σx exactly), and Azuma–Hoeffding gives |Σx − fl(Σx)| ≤ u·‖x‖₂·√(c·log(1/δ)) with probability 1−δ. A *probabilistic* contract (ε, δ) instead of a deterministic one — worth having as a first-class category since it's the right tool for long training-loop sums where fp32 itself drifts.

## 2. Quantization with computable elementwise bounds

- **Block-scaled quantization (your `mxfp4_moe_quant`)**: nearest-rounding to the E2M1 grid with scale 2^e gives per-element |ΔA| ≤ half-grid-gap = 2^e — and 2^e is *literally stored in the ue8m0 scale byte*, so the bound is recoverable at runtime from metadata alone. That's the key property to write down: **bound computable from the compressed representation, no reference needed**.
- **Linear propagation through GEMM**: since Y = AB is linear in each operand, |ΔY[i,j]| ≤ δA·‖B[:,j]‖₁ + δB·‖A[i,:]‖₁ + K·δA·δB. Provable, cheap to evaluate from one pass over the operands. This is the bound that justifies W4A4 end-to-end.
- **Error feedback / residual coding** for lossy allreduce or cross-node KV transfer: carry the quantization residual, re-quantize residual+update next round → the dropped signal telescopes, accumulated error ≤ last quantizer's step bound. Gives *lossy transport with bounded, non-growing* end error.

## 3. Discrete relaxations (selection, sampling)

- **Gap analysis for top-k / argmax** — very relevant to `dsa_topk_logits`: if each computed logit ẑ satisfies |ẑ − z| ≤ b (via γ_D on the fp8 path), and the gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th true logits is g > 2b, then **the top-k selection is provably identical to exact fp32 selection**. A relaxed numeric path with *zero* output error whenever the margin condition holds; you can even measure the margin at runtime.
- **Softmax tail truncation**: dropping keys with z ≤ z_max − τ makes the dropped probability mass ≤ (n_dropped)·e⁻τ; attention output is a convex combination of V rows, so ‖Δout‖ ≤ TV-mass · max‖vⱼ‖. Provable sparsification for `dsa_sparse_fwd`.
- **Approximate-top-k contracts**: define the indexer contract as "selected-set score ≥ α · optimal" (or every retained logit ≥ τ) rather than exact argpartition — the relaxation becomes a spec, testable directly.
- **Random projections for logits** (JL): |⟨Rx, Ry⟩ − ⟨x, y⟩| ≤ ε‖x‖‖y‖ w.p. 1−δ for m = O(log(n/δ)/ε²) — shrinks the D in your indexer's QKᵀ while keeping the top-k *gap condition* verifiable.
- **Sampled reductions**: Hoeffding gives (ε, δ) bounds for subsampled sums; median-of-means tightens the δ.

## 4. Communication / scheduling contracts

- **Staleness bounds**: s-stale reads in the overlap executor are a *provable* contract for ρ-contraction iterations (Bertsekas–Tsitsiklis async convergence) — worth writing down as the formal model for pipeline overlap, even if you only ever cite the theorem rather than apply it to training.
- **Mass-conserving drops**: top-k sparsification with contract Σ(dropped) ≤ ε·‖x‖₁ — bound verified cheaply on-device.

## 5. How the bounds get proven (the meta-techniques)

- **Backward error**: fl(f(x)) = f(x + Δx) with ‖Δx‖ ≤ γ_n‖x‖ — often the cleanest way to compose: downstream sees only a slightly perturbed input.
- **Lipschitz/induced-norm composition through kernels**: softmax logit perturbation → ‖Δp‖₁ ≤ 2‖Δz‖∞; V perturbation → |Δout| ≤ max_j‖Δv_j‖. These two compose your quantization bounds through an entire attention block.
- **Exhaustive enumeration for tiny formats**: a single fp4×fp4→fp32 op has 16×16 input pairs — the bound is *machine-checked*, not estimated. Same trick for one MMA instruction at fp8.
- **Interval arithmetic** for closed-form functions (exp2, rsqrt) — rigorous enclosures.
- **Monte-Carlo certification** for probabilistic contracts: report (ε, δ) with the concentration inequality backing it.

## Suggested shape for `relex/`

1. `TECHNIQUES.md` — the catalog above, one section per category, each entry: *relaxation → bound → proof technique → where it applies in vkernels*.
2. `bounds.py` — small pure functions that compute the bounds at runtime: `gamma(n, u)`, `mxfp4_element_bound(scale_bytes)`, `gemm_output_bound(δA, δB, ...)`, `topk_gap_threshold(b)`. These are testable against your CPU oracles, which fits the repo's culture.
3. Optionally a per-kernel "relaxed contract" table replacing bit-identity where a derivation exists (split-K reductions, atomics, W4A4 MoE, fp8 indexer).

Ranked by (perf headroom × bound strength) ÷ adoption cost, grounded in what's actually on the critical path in this repo:

## 1. Convexity bounds on attention output — the biggest direct win

`dsa_sparse_fwd` is KV-traffic bound (HBM at decode, RDMA cross-node). The convex-combination argument gives you a *continuous, certified* sparsity/compression knob:

> output error ≤ (dropped probability mass) × max‖v_j‖

- Softmax tail truncation τ converts directly into skipped KV tile reads — bytes saved scale linearly with e⁻τ, and the bound is tight, not loose.
- The same argument covers quantizing V (bound = max‖Δv‖ per element, no gap analysis needed).
- It composes: indexer gap condition (selection invariance) + tail truncation + V quantization all chain through one Lipschitz story.

This is the only technique on the list where the bound directly licenses a *new* kernel-level optimization with measurable GB/s payoff, rather than certifying something you already do.

## 2. Gap analysis for the top-k indexer — the best effort-to-value

Your fp8 indexer (`dsa_topk_logits`, e4m3fnuz) is already approximate with no correctness story. The gap condition — *selection provably identical to fp32 whenever logit margin > 2·γ_D* — is nearly free to implement (one bound function + a margin you can even log at runtime) and upgrades an existing approximation to **zero-error-under-condition**. It also licenses going *further*: shrinking D, JL-projecting the indexer, or coarsening precision while keeping the exact-selection guarantee. Best first entry for `relex/`.

## 3. γ_K tolerance classes — the multiplier

Today's contracts say "bit-identical to CPU oracle," which is exactly what blocks split-K reductions, atomic accumulation, and FMA-contraction freedom on device. Replacing bit-identity with a *derived* γ bound costs nothing and unlocks every order-sensitive optimization. No direct perf, but it removes a constraint that currently fights your kernel tuning ladder.

## 4. MXFP4 bound-from-scale-bytes — documentation value

W4A4 is already shipped; the win is that the error bound is recoverable from the ue8m0 bytes alone, so per-group adaptive precision becomes certifiable. Mostly verification, some future headroom.

## 5. Lossy cross-node KV — largest absolute win, hardest sell

Cross-node restore is pinned at ~88.5 GB/s fused vs a 220–243 GB/s roofline, and RDMA is worse — a 2–4× byte cut with a per-element Δ/2 bound is the biggest raw perf on the table. But the current acceptance criteria are explicitly *byte-identical*, and it's the most end-quality-visible change. Do it last, with the error-feedback variant so the residual is provably non-accumulating.

**Recommendation:** start `relex/` with #2 (gap analysis) as the proof-of-concept — smallest code, hard guarantee, immediately useful — then build #1 (attention convexity bounds) as the flagship with a `bounds.py` that computes truncation thresholds from a target output tolerance. #3 falls out almost for free once the γ machinery exists.
what's information-theory bounded and backed approach that we can learn from?

Information theory gives you the *other half* of the relex story: numerical analysis bounds say "how much error this operation adds"; information theory says "what's the cheapest possible representation for a given error budget, and when are you at the optimum." Here's the landscape worth learning from, mapped to this repo:

## A. Rate–distortion theory — the master framework

**R(D)** = minimum bits/element for distortion ≤ D. Everything else is a special case.

- **The high-rate quantization law**: D ≈ c·σ²·2^(−2R) — every extra bit quarters MSE (the "6 dB/bit" SQNR rule). Tells you the *exchange rate* between bits and error before you write any code.
- **Reverse water-filling** (Gaussian sources): the RD-optimal bit allocation across independent groups is *rate ∝ log-variance*. Your MXFP4 per-group ue8m0 scale bytes are already carrying the per-group σ — the RD view tells you when fixed-rate E2M1-everywhere is leaving distortion on the table, and how to allocate mixed 4/6/8-bit formats across groups under a global D budget.
- **Lloyd–Max**: the optimal scalar quantizer for a fixed rate — the principled upgrade path for KV/activation quantizers.

*Learn from:* Shannon (1959) rate–distortion; Cover & Thomas ch. 10; Gray & Neuhoff, "Quantization" (IEEE TIT 1998) — the definitive survey.

## B. Distortion measured in task space — the bridge to proven output bounds

The key move: define D over *attention/output distributions*, not stored values.

- **Chain**: bits → KL(full ‖ compressed) → Pinsker: TV ≤ √(KL/2) → attention output error ≤ TV · max‖v‖ (the convexity bound from before). Now a compression ratio maps to a certified model-output bound.
- **Data processing inequality**: information only degrades through processing, so the chain composes layer by layer without new assumptions — the information-theoretic analogue of your Lipschitz composition.

*Learn from:* Pinsker/Vajda inequalities; Csiszár & Körner for the heavy machinery.

## C. Information bottleneck — principled "what to keep"

- Compress X while preserving I(X; Y). For the DSA indexer: top-k selection is a heuristic; IB gives the objective "keep the KV tiles maximizing mutual information with the next-token distribution," with rate = KV bytes. The gap analysis from before is the zero-error limit of this; IB is the budgeted version.

*Learn from:* Tishby, Pereira & Bialek (1999).

## D. Method of types / large deviations — certifying probabilistic contracts

- All the (ε, δ) guarantees (sampled reductions, stochastic rounding, Monte-Carlo certification) are finite-sample shadows of Sanov/Hoeffding, whose exponents *are* KL divergences — and these exponents are provably tight. So your probabilistic contracts aren't just valid, they're near-optimal in sample complexity.
- **Dithered quantization** (Schuchman): adding known dither makes quantization error uniform, input-independent, and exactly bounded — the communications-engineering ancestor of stochastic rounding, with the cleanest proofs.

## E. Lower bounds — knowing when to stop

- **JL is bits-optimal**: preserving n dot products to ε needs Ω(log n/ε²) dimensions (packing/Fano argument). When you shrink the indexer head dim, you're provably at the floor — no clever scheme does better in general.
- **Fano's inequality**: below some bit budget, top-k selection *must* err. Useful to know when someone proposes "just use 2-bit logits."

## F. Distributed source coding — for the KV restore/donate path

- **Slepian–Wolf / Wyner–Ziv**: when the decoder has correlated side information (stale peer pages in cross-node KV reuse), you can encode at ≈ conditional entropy with provably small rate penalty. Delta-encoding donations against the receiver's old copy is the practical embodiment; bound = quantizer step, rate ≈ H(new | old).

## G. The synthesis worth stealing: rate–distortion–compute

Treat **bytes moved** and **FLOPs done** as two rate currencies, output error as the distortion budget D, and allocate optimally: e.g., RD logic says spend precision on V before K when the attention-output Lipschitz constants differ; spend KV bytes before indexer FLOPs when the exponents differ. That's exactly the decision structure `relex` needs — a principled way to answer "where does the next marginal byte/FLOP buy the most fidelity?"

| relex target | IT framework | bound you get |
|---|---|---|
| MXFP4 group formats | reverse water-filling, Lloyd–Max | global D budget, optimal bit mix |
| KV cross-node lossy transfer | R(D) + Wyner–Ziv vs stale pages | bits ↔ certified output error |
| DSA top-k indexer | IB + JL optimality + Fano floor | selection-optimality, head-dim floor |
| Sparse attention τ | Pinsker + convexity | mass budget ↔ output error |
| Stochastic rounding / sampling | Sanov, dithering | tight (ε, δ) exponents |

# relex — information-theoretic foundations for relaxed correctness

`relex` is the home for techniques that relax kernel correctness in exchange
for speed, bytes, or FLOPs — **with a proven bound on the resulting error**,
not an empirically observed one.

This README covers the *information-theoretic half* of that story. The two
halves answer different questions:

* **Numerical analysis** (companion note, to be written): *how much error does
  this operation add?* — unit roundoff, Wilkinson `γ_n` bounds, quantization
  step bounds, Lipschitz composition.
* **Information theory** (this document): *what is the cheapest possible
  representation for a given error budget — and when are we already at the
  optimum?* Rate–distortion says what the floor is; lower-bound theorems say
  when no scheme can do better; distortion chains convert a compression ratio
  into a certified model-output error.

Together they give `relex` its contract shape: **(R, D)** — *N bits per
element, with output error ≤ D* — instead of "bit-identical to the CPU
oracle".

---

## 1. The master framework: rate–distortion

Rate–distortion theory (Shannon 1959) defines **R(D)**: the minimum average
bits per sample needed to represent a source within distortion D. Every
compression decision in a kernel stack is an R(D) problem in disguise — the
question is only whether the distortion is measured honestly.

Three results translate directly into kernel terms.

**The high-rate exchange rate.** For a scalar quantizer at R bits per
element, high-rate theory gives

```text
D ≈ c · σ² · 2^(−2R)
```

i.e. *one extra bit quarters the MSE* (the "≈ 6 dB per bit" SQNR rule).
This is the exchange rate between bits and error before any code is written:
cutting KV cache from 16 bits to 8 costs a factor ~256 in elementwise MSE —
whether that matters is decided downstream, in task-space distortion
(§2), not here.

**Reverse water-filling.** For independent Gaussian groups with variances
σᵢ², the R(D)-optimal rate allocation is

```text
Rᵢ = max(0, ½·log₂(σᵢ²/θ))        θ chosen so ΣRᵢ = R
```

Bits go to high-variance groups first, ∝ log-variance. Our MXFP4 per-group
ue8m0 scale bytes already carry a per-group σ estimate — a fixed E2M1 grid
everywhere is a fixed-rate allocation that reverse water-filling says is
suboptimal whenever group variances spread. The RD view licenses *mixed
4/6/8-bit group formats under one global D budget* and says how to allocate.

**Lloyd–Max.** The optimal scalar quantizer at a fixed rate (centroids at
conditional means, decision levels halfway between). This is the principled
upgrade path for activation/KV quantizers beyond uniform grids, and it
composes with the scale-byte machinery we already ship: per-group data,
better codebooks.

> Reading: Shannon, *Coding theorems for a discrete source with a fidelity
> criterion* (1959) · Cover & Thomas, *Elements of Information Theory*, ch. 10
> · Gray & Neuhoff, *Quantization*, IEEE T-IT (1998).

## 2. Distortion in task space: the bound chain

The single most useful idea to steal: **define D over model outputs, not
stored values.** A KV entry compressed to 8 bits has a large elementwise
error and possibly a tiny attention-output error — the second number is the
one that is a contract.

For attention the chain is explicit. Let P be the full attention
distribution and Q the compressed/sparse one; V the value rows:

```text
bits spent ──►  KL(P ‖ Q)  ──Pinsker──►  TV(P, Q) ≤ √(KL/2)
                                     ──convexity──►  |Δout| ≤ TV · diam(V)
```

* **Convexity step:** attention output is a convex combination of value rows,
  so replacing P by Q moves the output by at most `TV(P,Q) · max_{i,j}‖v_i − v_j‖`.
  No assumptions on V, no gap analysis, one line.
* **Data processing inequality (DPI):** for any downstream map T,
  `KL(T(P) ‖ T(Q)) ≤ KL(P ‖ Q)`. The chain composes layer by layer without
  new hypotheses — the information-theoretic counterpart of Lipschitz
  composition, and the reason an end-to-end bound can be stated once, at the
  representation, and trusted everywhere below.

Everything in §1 plugs in here: a quantizer's D (measured as KL between
attention logits/distributions, not as elementwise MSE) is what the budget
means, and Pinsker converts it back to the `‖Δout‖` norms the kernels and
tests already speak.

Related: the **rate–distortion–perception** tradeoff (Blau & Michaeli)
formalizes the choice of distortion metric itself — perceptual/task metrics
vs. signal metrics — which is exactly the decision when a contract should be
KL-in-distribution rather than L∞-in-value.

## 3. Information bottleneck: what to keep

Rate–distortion with a relevance variable: compress X while preserving
`I(X; Y)` (Tishby, Pereira & Bialek 1999). In kernel terms: **the KV tiles,
tokens, or experts we keep should maximize mutual information with the
next-token distribution**, with rate = bytes retained.

This is the principled version of the DSA indexer's top-k selection. The
*zero-error limit* of this idea is logit gap analysis (approximate logits
with margin > 2·bound select provably the same set); the *budgeted version*
is the information bottleneck — keep what carries information about Y, drop
what doesn't, at a rate the byte budget sets.

## 4. Probabilistic contracts: method of types and dithering

Every `(ε, δ)` guarantee we would ever print on a kernel — sampled
reductions, stochastic rounding, Monte-Carlo certification — is a
finite-sample shadow of large-deviation theory, and the exponents there are
*information divergences*:

* **Sanov / Hoeffding:** `P(empirical ≉ truth) ≈ 2^(−n·KL)`. The bounds are
  tight in the exponent, so these contracts are not merely valid — they are
  near-optimal in sample count. The gap between Hoeffding and the true
  exponent is itself measured by a KL term, which is why empirical-Bernstein
  refinements exist.
* **Dithered quantization** (Schuchman): adding known uniform dither makes
  quantization error exactly uniform and input-independent — the
  communications-engineering ancestor of stochastic rounding, with the
  cleanest proofs and a hard per-element bound `|Δ| ≤ Δ_step/2` that still
  holds on top of the stochastic ones.

## 5. Lower bounds: knowing when to stop

The other half of "proven" is knowing when nothing better exists.

* **JL is bits-optimal.** Preserving all pairwise dot products of n vectors
  to relative error ε requires `Ω(log(n)/ε²)` dimensions (packing/Fano
  argument). When we shrink the indexer head dimension with a random
  projection, we are provably at the floor — no scheme beats it in general.
* **Fano's inequality.** Below a certain bit budget, top-k selection *must*
  err: the information about the ranking simply isn't in the bits. The
  useful form: it tells us when a "2-bit indexer logits" proposal is not an
  engineering problem but an impossibility.

Together with §1 these make the `relex` claims two-sided: *this scheme
achieves D at rate R* AND *no scheme achieves D at much less than R*.

## 6. Distributed source coding: the KV restore/donate path

When the decoder holds correlated side information — stale peer pages in
cross-node KV reuse (docs/comm-cross-node-kv.md), or the previous layer's
cache — the encoder need not send what the receiver can reconstruct:

* **Slepian–Wolf:** lossless coding with decoder side information achieves
  `H(X | Y)` — the conditional entropy — without the encoder knowing Y.
* **Wyner–Ziv:** the lossy version; the rate penalty for keeping side
  information decoder-only is provably small (≤ ½ bit/sample for
  Gaussian–MSE sources; Zamir 1996).

Delta-encoding a donation against the receiver's stale copy is the practical
embodiment: rate ≈ `H(new | old)`, bound = the quantizer step. This is the
certified-lossy version of the currently byte-exact cross-node path: same
kernel interface, a `(R, D)` contract instead of byte-identity.

## 7. Synthesis: rate–distortion–compute

The operational takeaway for this repo: treat **bytes moved** and **FLOPs
done** as two rate currencies, output error as the distortion budget, and
allocate between them by marginal distortion reduction:

* spend precision on V before K when the output-Lipschitz constants differ
  (§2 makes both measurable — TV of the attention weights vs. value
  diameter);
* spend KV bytes before indexer FLOPs when the exponents in §5/§1 differ;
* spend bits where reverse water-filling points (§1), not uniformly.

That is the decision structure `relex` exists to support — a principled
answer to "where does the next marginal byte or FLOP buy the most fidelity?"

---

## Mapping to vkernels

| target (existing kernel/doc) | IT framework | contract you can print |
|---|---|---|
| `mxfp4_moe_quant` group formats | reverse water-filling, Lloyd–Max | global D budget over a mixed-bit allocation |
| `dsa_topk_logits` (fp8 indexer) | information bottleneck; JL optimality; Fano floor | selection-optimality objective; provable head-dim floor |
| `dsa_sparse_fwd` (sparse attention, τ) | Pinsker + convexity chain | dropped-mass budget ↔ certified `‖Δout‖` |
| cross-node KV restore/donate | R(D) + Wyner–Ziv vs stale pages | bits ↔ certified output error |
| lossy allreduce / stochastic rounding | dithering; Sanov exponents | `(ε, δ)` contracts with near-tight exponents |

## Reading order

1. Cover & Thomas, *Elements of Information Theory* — ch. 10 (rate–distortion),
   ch. 11 (method of types); skim ch. 7 (DPI, Pinsker).
2. Gray & Neuhoff, *Quantization* (1998) — everything about §1 in practice.
3. Blau & Michaeli — the rate–distortion–perception tradeoff (choosing D).
4. Tishby, Pereira & Bialek (1999) — the information bottleneck.
5. Zamir (1996) — Wyner–Ziv rate loss; then Slepian–Wolf/Wyner–Ziv originals
   as needed for §6.

A companion note will cover the numerical-analysis side (γ-bounds, quantization
step bounds, Lipschitz composition, gap analysis) and the `bounds.py` helpers
that evaluate both halves at runtime.
